title: Elucidating Processes at Hard-Soft Interfaces in Next-Generation Electrochemical Devices by Cryogenic Electron Microscopy
content: The key to enabling many revolutionary, next-generation electrochemical energy devices lies in understanding fundamental processes that occur on the nanoscale at interfaces between various materials within these devices [1, 2]. For example, alkali-metal batteries have the potential to provide dramatically improved energy density over current technologies, but are limited by processes at electrode-electrolyte interfaces that are not well understood and lead to rapid capacity fade and safety concerns. Use of specialized electrolyte materials, such as inflammable polymers, can help to improve the safety of these devices, but rapid capacity fade remains a challenge due to a variety of poorly understood polymer-electrode interfacial processes [3]. Furthermore, low-temperature hydrogen devices that use polymer membranes to conduct ions have the potential to be a disruptive technology for converting water to hydrogen, which can then be used to help stabilize the electrical grid, provide high heat for industrial processes, and power heavy-duty vehicles [4, 5]. While commercial products have been produced, fundamental understanding of interfacial processes involving nm-scale ionomer thin films and support/catalyst materials is lacking [6], limiting various properties of these devices and preventing them from being widely adopted. In both cases, nm-scale information about the structure, composition, and bonding occurring at the hard-soft interfaces within the devices is crucial for truly understanding subsequently controlling the processes that occur there. Due to the buried and highly beam-sensitive nature of the materials and interfaces in these devices, however, conventional electron microscopy techniques are insufficient for providing information about the native nanoscale properties of these interfaces.
